title: Short Stuff: Nero and His Fiddle
summary: Short Stuff episode revisiting the myth that Emperor Nero fiddled while Rome burned during the Great Fire of 64 CE. Josh and Chuck (with Jerry sitting in for Dave) recall Josh's old HowStuffWorks article. They cover the fire's scale (six days, most of the city destroyed, about half a million people homeless per Tacitus), rumors that Nero set the fire, his rebuilding, the blame-shifting persecution of Christians including Paul and Peter, the claim that the fiddle did not exist yet, Nero's real playing of the scythara and his music competitions, his relief efforts after the fire, historian Mary Frances Gilliam's reading of "fiddling" as wasting time, and Nero's suicide about four years later. The episode ends with a tangent about the TV show Star City and a sign-off.

segments.title: The Great Fire of Rome
segments.summary: The fire burned for six days and seven nights in 64 CE, destroying about seventy percent of the city; Tacitus reported roughly half a million people left homeless.

segments.title: Rumors that Nero set the fire
segments.summary: Rumors spread that the government was involved; Nero was the prime suspect and rebuilt Rome in a style he preferred, which fueled the blame.

segments.title: Origin of the fiddling story
segments.summary: The fiddling story grew out of the rumor that Nero watched the city burn while playing an instrument.

segments.title: Persecution of Christians and the fiddle myth
segments.summary: Nero blamed Christians and persecuted them, including the executions of Paul and Peter. Chuck says no fiddle existed then, since the instrument arrived around the eleventh century; Josh notes Nero played the scythara and held music competitions the Senate disliked.

segments.title: Nero's relief efforts after the fire
segments.summary: Nero returned from Antium, coordinated firefighting, opened public buildings and gardens for shelter, and sold imported grain cheaply. Popularity among commoners is noted, and the Senate is suggested as the source of the propaganda.

segments.title: Mary Frances Gilliam and the meaning of fiddling
segments.summary: Historian Mary Frances Gilliam of the University of North Carolina suggested fiddling can mean wasting time or futzing around, not just playing a violin. The hosts connect this to Senate criticism that Nero's response was inadequate.

segments.title: Nero's reputation and his death
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh note Nero's other crimes, including his mother's killing and the use of wild animals in executions. The Senate declared Nero a public enemy after the army turned against him, and he took his own life about four years after the fire.

segments.title: Tangent on Star City and sign-off
segments.summary: Off-topic chat about the TV show Star City, a Soviet-perspective space race drama with British actors, and the hosts close the short.
